extra.message: A Supabase client is being constructed with a service_role key read from SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY. Same risk as the TypeScript/JS version of this rule: service_role bypasses RLS on every table unconditionally, so any per-caller authorization this code needs has to be enforced in Python, not left to the database. Real example already in this repo: tools/supabase/client.py's CommanderSupabaseClient reads SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY into self.key and passes it straight to create_client() with no scoping. Contrast with telegram-bots/xo/scoped_supabase.py, which documents (in its own module docstring, citing the Chief Engineer's xo-bot-service-role-decision.md) a deliberate, reviewed decision to move a similar bot off service_role onto a scoped Postgres role — that write-up is the right model for triaging a hit from this rule: is the broad access actually needed and reviewed, or should this be narrower?

A Supabase/PostgREST filter (.or()/.ilike()/.filter()/.match()) is being built from a template literal containing an interpolated value. Supabase's PostgREST filter syntax is itself a small query language (operators, commas, and parentheses are meaningful), so an unescaped, user-controlled value placed inside one of these strings can widen the filter beyond what was intended (e.g. inject `,other_column.eq.x` to add another OR-branch, or unbalanced parens to change grouping) — RLS row policies still apply, but the filter the app THINKS it is sending and the filter PostgREST actually receives can diverge. Real examples of this exact shape already exist in this repo, e.g. lcars-portal/src/app/api/health-osint/library/route.ts (`query.or(\`title.ilike.%${q}%,description.ilike.%${q}%\`)`, `q` is a raw searchParams value) and lcars-portal/src/lib/ask.ts. Prefer chained, parameterized filter calls (.ilike('title', pattern)) or Supabase's `.or()` with values passed as separate arguments/bind params over building the filter string yourself; at minimum, strip/escape `,()."'` from any value before interpolating it into one of these calls.

A Supabase client is being constructed with SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY. The service_role key bypasses Row Level Security entirely on every table, not just the ones this code path intends to touch — so any authorization this route is supposed to enforce (e.g. "this row belongs to the requesting user/session") has to be implemented explicitly in application code, because the database will not do it for a service_role query. This repo already has ~15+ Next.js API routes under lcars-portal/src/app/api/** that build a fresh service_role client inline per-route (see lcars-portal/src/lib/supabase-service-role.ts's own docstring, which documents exactly this bypass for core_events). This rule is advisory, not proof of a bug: confirm the route (a) checks requireSession()/an equivalent auth check before this client is used, and (b) either has no notion of per-row ownership (fine) or explicitly re-checks ownership itself (e.g. `.eq('user_id', session.user.id)`) before using this client to read/update/delete a row addressed by caller-supplied input (a route param, a body field) — RLS will not catch a missing check here the way it would for an anon/authenticated client.

Real examples of this exact shape already exist in this repo, e.g. lcars-portal/src/app/api/health-osint/library/route.ts (`query.or(\`title.ilike.%${q}%,description.ilike.%${q}%\`)`, `q` is a raw searchParams value) and lcars-portal/src/lib/ask.ts. Prefer chained, parameterized filter calls (.ilike('title', pattern)) or Supabase's `.or()` with values passed as separate arguments/bind params over building the filter string yourself; at minimum, strip/escape `,()."'` from any value before interpolating it into one of these calls.
